planting.note: Direct-sow in fall with 6-8 weeks cold stratification into gritty, fast-draining soil; standing winter wet is the main failure risk, not drought.

directions: A striking pink-and-yellow bicolor columbine endemic to oil-shale cliffs and talus of the Green River Formation in northeastern Utah and western Colorado, this species blooms for up to eight weeks and tolerates poor, alkaline soils and high altitude. Because it evolved on crumbly shale cliffs, give it gritty, fast-draining soil even though it tolerates clay — a rock garden or scree bed suits it better than rich perennial border soil. Deadhead to extend the long bloom window, and expect self-sown seedlings nearby since it hybridizes readily with other columbines grown close by.

planting.note: Direct-sow outdoors in fall/winter for natural cold stratification into a part-shade site that stays evenly cool and slightly moist at the root zone, mimicking its native hanging-garden seep habitat.

directions: A compact, nodding red-and-yellow columbine from hanging-garden seeps and limestone canyon walls of Arizona, New Mexico, and Utah, this species is hummingbird-pollinated and deer-resistant, with a tidier habit than showier hybrid columbines. Recreate its native seep microclimate with a part-shade site that stays evenly cool and slightly moist rather than a hot open bed. Buy seed labeled with a known wild collection locality to avoid confusion with closely related look-alikes, since it sits very close taxonomically to Aquilegia formosa.

planting.note: Sow in spring where water collects briefly after rain or near a drip line, not in open unamended desert soil; an early indoor start can flower in its first year.

directions: A gray-green-leaved, red-and-yellow columbine from Mojave Desert mountain seeps and canyon walls, this species is more alkaline-tolerant than most columbines and goes stress-deciduous through heat and drought swings rather than dying outright. Despite its desert origin it is a seep-and-spring-margin specialist, not a true xerophyte, so site it where moisture collects rather than in open desert soil. Its notable tolerance for alkaline, sandy, or poorly drained soil makes it a useful option for hard-water regions and limestone gardens where typical columbines struggle.

planting.note: Sow fresh seed in a cold frame as soon as ripe into cool, open-woodland soil; germination is slow and erratic and often doesn't occur until the following spring.

directions: A cold-hardy, blue-and-white boreal columbine ranging from Alberta and Alaska south into Montana, Wyoming, and the Dakotas, this species carries short-spurred, smaller flowers and a tidy habit suited to rock gardens and cold-climate native plantings. Treat it as a woodland-edge plant rather than a sun perennial, since hot afternoon sun is its main failure point in warmer gardens. It is short-lived but self-seeds prolifically where happy, so grow it apart from other columbine species if self-sown seedlings should stay true to type.
